AI lowers those barriers dramatically, allowing smaller candidates, grassroots organizations, and individual citizens to produce compelling rebuttals or alternative framings. Restricting the technology concentrates power in the hands of those who can afford compliance and legal defense. Each innovation eventually integrated into the normal rough-and-tumble of politics. Deepfakes will follow the same trajectory unless regulators intervene to freeze the medium at an early stage. Preserving unrestricted use of AI-generated deepfakes and similar media requires active resistance to any regulatory regime that subordinates political speech to notions of authenticity. Such restrictions trade short-term comfort for long-term erosion of the expressive liberties that enable accountability. A vibrant democracy tolerates the discomfort of contested representations because it prefers an unruly public debate to a managed one. One of the most enduring justifications for protecting seemingly harmful speech is the concept of the "marketplace of ideas," first articulated by philosopher John Stuart Mill. Throughout history, each major advancement in communication technology has sparked fears about its potential for abuse. The printing press was accused of spreading heresy; radio was blamed for corrupting youth culture; television was said to dumb down intellectual discourse. Attempts to regulate political speech—especially when cloaked in the language of protecting democracy—can quickly spiral into broader censorship efforts.
